questions.title: What does "strict adherence" mean in Louisiana insurance cancellation law, and why didn't the missing signature violate it?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Louisiana cases saying that "strict adherence" to statutory cancellation procedures is required, and that "any defect in this process results in an ineffective cancellation." But then the court says the lack of a signature on the certification doesn't violate the statute because the statute doesn't explicitly require one. How does this square with the strict adherence standard? If courts require strict adherence, shouldn't that mean the finance company needs to strictly follow every detail? Is there a difference between "strict adherence" and adding requirements that aren't in the text?

questions.title: Can a computer system's automated receipt satisfy a statutory "receipt" requirement?
questions.question_body: The statute requires that "[u]pon receipt of such notice of cancellation and statement from the premium finance company, the insurer shall consider that cancellation... has been requested." Here, GoAuto's computer system automatically received the email at midnight and immediately cancelled the policy, with no human involvement until hours later. The court says this satisfies "receipt" because "company computers do much that individuals once did." But the statute was presumably written with human receipt in mind. Is there a limit to this reasoning? Could any automated process satisfy statutory requirements meant for humans? What if the statute had said "upon receiving" instead of "upon receipt" - would that change the analysis?

questions.title: Why did the court say a signature isn't required when Benitez mentioned signature absence as a defect?
questions.question_body: The court cites Benitez v. Elsayed, where the court noted that the notice "is not signed by any individual, and does not purport to 'certify' any of the statements contained therein." The current court says Benitez didn't hold that lack of signature alone would invalidate cancellation. But I'm confused - if strict adherence is required, and Benitez listed the missing signature as part of what made the notice defective, why doesn't that suggest a signature is required? Is the court distinguishing Benitez correctly, or is it minimizing what that case implied about signatures?

questions.title: What standard governs when federal courts should certify questions to state supreme courts?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs asked the Fifth Circuit to certify the statutory interpretation questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, but the court declined, quoting Jefferson v. Lead Industry Association that certification is important and they won't "go to that well too often." The court also said that a term being undefined by the state supreme court "is not sufficient to warrant certification." But these seem like genuinely novel questions about Louisiana insurance law that could affect many policies. What makes a certification request compelling enough for a federal court to actually grant it? Is the court being too restrictive here given that Louisiana's insurance industry is heavily regulated and these procedural questions matter?

questions.title: Does the timing of the signature stamp matter if certification was already electronically sent?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the timeline here. APAC's computer sends an email with the certification statement (unsigned), GoAuto's computer receives it and cancels the policy, and THEN an APAC employee applies a signature stamp to printed documents. The court seems to say the signature isn't required at all - but if it WERE required, wouldn't the timing be fatal? And doesn't the fact that they apply the signature stamp later suggest even APAC thought some signed documentation was necessary? Why does the later signature stamp exist at all if the court says no signature is required?

questions.title: Why did the appellate court decline to address the district court's "private carrier" reasoning?
questions.question_body: The district court held alternatively that the APAC employee delivering physical documents was a "private carrier" under the statute. The appellate court called this "imaginative and unconventional" and declined to consider it because they found the email satisfied the statute. I thought appellate courts could affirm on any ground supported by the record. But don't they also sometimes address alternative holdings to provide guidance? If the "private carrier" definition is important for future cases, wouldn't addressing it be valuable? Also, what exactly is a "private carrier" in this context - does it just mean any delivery service that isn't the postal service?

questions.title: How does Erie doctrine apply when federal courts interpret undefined state statutory terms?
questions.question_body: This case involves a federal court interpreting Louisiana's insurance finance statute, La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550, which has never been interpreted by Louisiana's highest court on these specific issues. Under Erie, federal courts sitting in diversity apply state substantive law. But when there's no state supreme court precedent, how should a federal court approach statutory interpretation? Should they be more cautious and certify? The court here uses general canons of statutory interpretation, but wouldn't Louisiana's own principles of statutory construction apply? How do federal courts determine what a state statute means when the state courts haven't spoken?
